title: The Cramming Student
briefing: Ines, 15, and her twin brother study the same 40 Spanish words for the same two hours in total. Ines does it all the night before the quiz; her brother does 20 minutes each evening for six days. Both ace the quiz the next morning — but a week later he remembers most of the words, and she remembers few.
question: Same words, same time — why did one twin's memory last and the other's fade?

clues.title: Same total time
clues.text: Both studied the same 40 words for two hours in total. Ines did it in one evening; her brother did 20 minutes each evening for six days.
clues.shows: the same amount of practice, split up differently

clues.title: Both aced day one
clues.text: On the quiz the next morning, they both scored over 90%. Ines had clearly learned the words.
clues.shows: cramming working fine in the short term

clues.title: A week later
clues.text: On a surprise quiz a week later, her brother remembers 34 of the words. Ines remembers 12.
clues.shows: the crammed memories fading much faster

visual.unit: words remembered a week later, Ines → brother

clues.title: Her turn to spread it out
clues.text: For the next unit Ines also does 20 minutes a day. A week later she remembers almost as many words as her brother.
clues.shows: the same person remembering far more once she spread out her practice

hypotheses.text: Ines is just worse at languages than her brother.
hypotheses.flaw: They scored the same on the next-morning quiz, and when Ines spread out her next unit she remembered almost as much as he did.

hypotheses.text: Spreading practice over several days, with sleep in between, makes the brain pull each word back up again and again; each recall after a gap makes the memory stronger and longer-lasting. Cramming fills a short-term memory that fades fast.
Ines got distracted by her phone while studying.
hypotheses.flaw: She aced the next-morning quiz, so she did learn the words — the difference only showed up a week later.

hypotheses.text: Studying at night is worse than studying in the day.
hypotheses.flaw: Her brother studied in the evenings too; what differed was spreading it over six days, not the time of day.

prediction.prompt: Ines studies for two hours in total. If she spreads those two hours over more and more days — from one night to a whole week — what happens to how many words she remembers a week later?

second.question: And her score on a quiz the very next morning after she finishes?

concepts.label: practice spread over days
concepts.hint: What did her brother do differently with the same two hours?

concepts.label: pulling it back up
concepts.hint: What does the brain have to do each time you come back to the words after a gap?

concepts.label: sleep in between
concepts.hint: What happens between each of her brother's sessions?

concepts.label: memory gets stronger
concepts.hint: What does each gap-and-recall do to the memory?

concepts.label: crammed memories fade
concepts.hint: What happened to Ines's words over the week?

transfer.context: Ollie learns a piano piece by practising 15 minutes a day for two weeks. His friend practises the same piece for 3½ hours the day before the recital. Both play well at the recital; a month later Ollie can still play it and his friend can't.
options: Spaced practice with sleep in between made Ollie's memory of the piece stronger and longer-lasting.
Ollie just has more natural talent.
His friend's piano was out of tune.
Recitals are easier for younger players.
transfer.retryHint: Same total practice, split up differently, and the gap only showing up later — which of Ines's clues set that up?
transfer.explanation: Ollie and his friend put in the same time. Ollie's fourteen short sessions made his brain pull the piece back up after a night's sleep again and again, strengthening it each time. His friend's single cram worked for the next day's recital and then faded — the same pattern as Ines and her brother.

takeaway: How you split your practice matters as much as how long you practise. Short sessions spread over days, with sleep in between, make your brain pull memories back again and again — and each time they get stronger. Cramming fades fast.
